Angle Bisector In Rectangle

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Drag the corners of a rectangle and watch a line split an angle into two equal parts.
How to play: Drag a corner or the point on the right side with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Check the equality to test what you see.
Look for the math

Draw a rectangle, pick a point on its right side and join two of its corners. You get an angle at one corner's opposite midpoint, and the middle line of the rectangle appears to cut it exactly in half. Is that always true?

The picture

ABCD is a rectangle: A top left, B bottom left, C bottom right, D top right. M is the midpoint of AD and N is the midpoint of BC, so MN is the line halfway across. P sits on the right side CD, and Q is where MP crosses the diagonal AC. The claim is that MN is the angle bisector of angle PNQ: angle QNM = angle MNP. That is exactly the equality the check button tests, in degrees, after each drag.

Two matching ratios

Let O be the centre of the rectangle, the midpoint of AC. Because MN is parallel to CD, triangles CPQ and OMQ are similar, giving

MP / MQ = CO / OQ.

Now take K on NQ so that KO is parallel to BC. Triangles CNQ and OKQ are similar too, so

CO / OQ = KN / KQ.

Putting those together gives MP / MQ = KN / KQ, which makes KM parallel to NP. The archived page prints MP/MQ = KN/NQ here; that is a slip of the pen (NQ instead of KQ). The logic test measures both: the printed ratio is not equal to MP/MQ, while the corrected one is, and it is the corrected one that yields the next step.

An isosceles triangle finishes it

O is the midpoint of MN and KO is perpendicular to MN, so K lies on the perpendicular bisector of MN. Hence KM = KN and triangle KMN is isosceles: angle KMN = angle KNM. Since KM is parallel to NP, the angle KMN equals the angle MNP. But K lies on NQ, so angle KNM is angle QNM. Therefore angle QNM = angle MNP. The hint button draws K and the two lines that make this visible.

Where the statement needs care

The old page just says "P lies on CD"; it does not say where. The equality above is true when P is above the middle of CD, which is where the applet puts P to begin with. Drag P below the middle and the ray NQ flips: the two angles then add to 180 degrees, so MN bisects the outside angle at N instead. At exactly the middle, MP is parallel to AC and Q does not exist. The logic test checks the page's equality on hundreds of rectangles with P above the middle, and the outside-angle relation on hundreds more below it, against a second transcription of the applet's own construction.

Try making the rectangle very wide, then very tall, and check the two angle readings each time. Then press Show hint to see the isosceles triangle behind them.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
